patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old woman with known NASH cirrhosis was brought to the emergency department by her daughter after two days of worsening confusion and slurred speech. Her daughter reports that the patient had been complaining of increased abdominal distension and had called her primary care provider about it three days ago. She had been told to increase her furosemide dose from 40 mg to 80 mg per day on her own, which she did. Over the following two days, she became progressively more confused, sleeping most of the day, mixing up names of grandchildren, and leaving the stove on twice. On the morning of admission, she called her daughter by the wrong name and did not recognize her son-in-law. She denied headache, fever, vision changes, or weakness. She denied chest pain or shortness of breath. She had been compliant with lactulose and rifaximin until two days ago when her daughter noticed she had forgotten multiple doses of lactulose. Her last bowel movement was two days ago. She had no recent travel, sick contacts, or dietary changes. She had been eating less than usual over the past week due to nausea. She has no history of seizures or alcohol use. Her prior hepatic encephalopathy episode six months ago had resolved with lactulose optimization over 48 hours. On review of her recent labs from one week prior, her potassium was borderline low at 3.4 mEq/L, and her creatinine was at her baseline of 1.0 mg/dL. Her family denies any falls, head trauma, or new medications.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), NASH cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) — precipitated by iatrogenic hypokalemia from excessive furosemide and lactulose non-adherence.

differential.key_features: CT/MRI to exclude; obesity/diabetes raise risk.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: K low; ammonia mildly elevated; cirrhosis features; glucose.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (AASLD/EASL HE; diuretic-induced hypokalemia and HE).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering furosemide (REDUCE), spironolactone, lactulose, rifaximin — restart and titrate; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — consider if no clinical improvement. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Consult hepatology — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.
Visual evoked potentials have no role in HE workup; no demyelinating process is on the differential.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: IV/PO potassium repletion (K target ≥4 mEq/L in HE).
Reduce furosemide dose to maintain spironolactone:furosemide ratio ~100:40 mg.
Restart lactulose 30 mL TID titrated to 2-4 stools/day; rifaximin 550 mg BID.
Patient education on lactulose adherence (titrate to stools, not 'as needed').
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not continue high-dose furosemide once K is depleted — diuretic regimen requires K monitoring.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
The 100:40 spironolactone-to-furosemide ratio maintains K balance in cirrhotic diuretic regimens.
Lactulose adherence is the single most common modifiable HE precipitant — counsel about titration to stools and not stopping when feeling well.
